title: Python for corpus work: count, sort, search, and show
summary: Write the code Kraus's homework asks for by yourself: loop over tagged (word, tag) pairs, count with a dictionary or Counter, sort to get a top-10 table, search with re (groups, backreferences, lookahead done right), turn counts into per-1,000 rates and TTR, and show results as a pandas table and a bar chart.
sourceNote: Built from the Ling 115 Python Refresher, Homework 1 (Gutenberg and Brown regex searches, -eth verbs, reduplication), Homework 2 (Brown top-10 words and tags, adverbs, the three tags of 'so'), and the Lecture 7 Brown corpus explorer (FreqDist, per-1,000 rates, TTR, keyness, bar charts). Sample data here is small and made up so it runs instantly; the code is the same you'd run on NLTK's corpora.

sections.heading: Every homework notebook has the same shape

blocks.md: Homework 1 and 2 look long, but every question is the same five steps: **get the words**, **loop** over them, **keep** the ones that match, **count** them, and **show** the top ones as a table. Learn those five and the homework stops being a wall of code.

columns: What it looks like in the homework
rows: `for word, tag in tagged:` / `for sent in ...:`

sections.heading: Printing a neat table with f-strings

blocks.body: Text with an `f` in front, where anything in `{curly braces}` is replaced by its value: `f"{word} {count}"`. Add `:15s` to pad text to 15 characters, `:>5` to right-align a number in 5, `:.2f` for 2 decimals.

blocks.title: The homework's table line
blocks.body:
word = "loveth"; count = 12
print(f"{word:15s} {count}")      ->   loveth          12
print(f"{word:>10} | {count:5d}")  ->       loveth |    12
print(f"{0.123456:.2f}")           ->   0.12
blocks.answer: `:15s` pads text to 15 characters, so the numbers line up in a column.

blocks.body: A pair like `("walked", "VBD")` can be split into two names in one go: `word, tag = pair`. In a loop: `for word, tag in tagged:` gives you both parts every round.
A one-line loop that builds a list: `[w.lower() for w, t in tagged if t == 'RB']` means "for every pair, if the tag is RB, keep the lowercased word".

blocks.body: A lookup table from keys to values: `counts = {"the": 2, "he": 3}`. `counts["he"]` gives 3. Perfect for "how many times did each word appear".

blocks.md: There are three ways to count with it. All three give the same answer; the last is shortest.

blocks.title: Three ways
blocks.body:
# 1. try / except (Homework 1 style)
try:
    counts[w] += 1
except KeyError:
    counts[w] = 1

# 2. .get with a default of 0
counts[w] = counts.get(w, 0) + 1

# 3. Counter does the whole loop for you
from collections import Counter
counts = Counter(words)
blocks.answer: `counts.get(w, 0)` means "the count so far, or 0 if this word is new".

sections.heading: Sorting to get a top-N list

blocks.body: Sorts anything. `key` says what to sort by; `key=lambda pair: pair[1]` means "by the second thing in each pair" (the count). `reverse=True` puts the biggest first.

blocks.title: Two ways to rank (word, count) pairs
blocks.body:
pairs = [("the", 3), ("back", 2), ("so", 3)]

sorted(pairs, key=lambda p: p[1], reverse=True)
  ->  [('the', 3), ('so', 3), ('back', 2)]

# Homework 1's trick: flip to (count, word) and sort that
sorted([(c, w) for w, c in pairs], reverse=True)
  ->  [(3, 'the'), (3, 'so'), (2, 'back')]
blocks.answer: Either works. `key=` keeps the pairs in (word, count) order.

sections.heading: Regex in Python: findall, finditer, compile

rows: A list of every matching piece of text
Each match as an object: `m.group()` is the text, `m.start()` where it starts
Save a pattern to reuse; then `pattern.finditer(text)`
Upper and lower case match alike
blocks.title: The four re functions from the Refresher

blocks.body: Matches the **edge of a word** (between a letter and a space or punctuation), without using up a character. `eth\b` means "eth at the end of a word".
Always write patterns as raw strings, `r'...'`. Without the `r`, Python turns `\b` into a backspace character before re ever sees it, and the pattern silently matches nothing.

blocks.title: Your turn: the -eth verbs
blocks.task: Homework 1, Problem 1.1: make `eth_words`, every word in `text` that **ends in eth**, using `re.findall` and `\b`.
blocks.setup:
# A few lines in the style of the Gutenberg texts
text = """He that loveth his brother abideth in the light. The Lord giveth and the Lord taketh away.
No, no, I will not go. She laughed and said very, very well. His teeth were white as snow.
Queen Elizabeth came on the twentieth day. The wind bloweth where it listeth.
Choo-choo went the little train, and the baby said night night."""
blocks.check:
import re
assert eth_words is not None, "Replace `None` with `re.findall(...)`."
exp = ["loveth", "abideth", "giveth", "taketh", "teeth", "Elizabeth", "twentieth", "bloweth", "listeth"]
assert list(eth_words) == exp, f"Expected {exp}. You have {eth_words}. Try r'[a-zA-Z]+eth\\b' (letters, then eth, then the end of the word)."
blocks.solution:
import re

eth_words = re.findall(r"[a-zA-Z]+eth\b", text)

print(eth_words)
hints: One or more letters is `[a-zA-Z]+`.
`re.findall(r"[a-zA-Z]+eth\b", text)`
blocks.success: It also caught teeth, Elizabeth and twentieth: spelling can't tell a verb from a noun. The next two sections fix that.

blocks.body: Parentheses in a pattern capture the part they wrap. `m.group(1)` is the text the first group matched.
Means "the **same text** group 1 matched, again". `(\w+) \1` matches a word followed by the same word: *night night*.

blocks.title: Your turn: reduplication
blocks.task: Homework 1, Problem 1.2: match a word repeated right after itself, allowing a **space**, a **comma and space**, or a **hyphen** in between (*no, no*, *very, very*, *choo-choo*, *night night*). Store all the full matches in `redups`.
blocks.starter:
import re

pattern = None   # r"..." with a group and \1
redups = [m.group() for m in re.finditer(pattern, text, flags=re.IGNORECASE)]

print(redups)
blocks.setup:
# A few lines in the style of the Gutenberg texts
text = """He that loveth his brother abideth in the light. The Lord giveth and the Lord taketh away.
No, no, I will not go. She laughed and said very, very well. His teeth were white as snow.
Queen Elizabeth came on the twentieth day. The wind bloweth where it listeth.
Choo-choo went the little train, and the baby said night night."""
blocks.check:
assert pattern is not None, "Write a pattern string."
assert redups == ["No, no", "very, very", "Choo-choo", "night night"], f"Expected ['No, no', 'very, very', 'Choo-choo', 'night night']. You have {redups}. The part between the two words can be ', ' or ' ' or '-': something like (, |-| )."
blocks.solution:
import re

pattern = r"\b(\w+)(, |-| )\1\b"
redups = [m.group() for m in re.finditer(pattern, text, flags=re.IGNORECASE)]

print(redups)
hints: Start with `r"\b(\w+) \1\b"`: word, space, same word.
Replace the space with a choice: `(, |-| )`. Order matters: try `, ` before ` `.
blocks.success: `\1` is the whole trick: a regex can't "remember" a word any other way. Note it still misses *the the* when the two copies differ in case unless you add `re.IGNORECASE`, which is why 'No, no' needed it.

sections.heading: Lookahead: excluding words, the right way

blocks.body: Checks that what comes **next** does **not** match `...`, without using up any text. Put it **before** the part it guards: `\b(?!teeth\b)[a-z]+eth\b` means "at the start of a word that isn't teeth, match an -eth word".

`[a-zA-Z]+(?!eth)` doesn't mean "words not ending in eth". The `+` grabs as many letters as it can, then the lookahead checks the text **after** the word (a space), which is never "eth", so it matches **every** word. The lookahead must sit at the **start** of the word, before the letters it's about.

blocks.title: Where the lookahead goes
blocks.body:
WRONG:  [a-zA-Z]+(?!eth)                 matches every word
RIGHT:  \b(?!(?:teeth|elizabeth)\b)[a-zA-Z]+eth\b
        ^ start of word, then "not teeth/elizabeth", then the -eth word
blocks.answer: Check at the start of the word, then match it.

blocks.title: Your turn: only the verbs
blocks.task: Make `verbs`: the **-eth** words in `text` **except** *teeth*, *Elizabeth*, and ordinal numbers ending in **-ieth** (twentieth, thirtieth). Use one pattern with negative lookahead(s) and `re.IGNORECASE`.
blocks.starter:
import re

pattern = None   # r"..."
verbs = re.findall(pattern, text, flags=re.IGNORECASE)

print(verbs)
blocks.setup:
# A few lines in the style of the Gutenberg texts
text = """He that loveth his brother abideth in the light. The Lord giveth and the Lord taketh away.
No, no, I will not go. She laughed and said very, very well. His teeth were white as snow.
Queen Elizabeth came on the twentieth day. The wind bloweth where it listeth.
Choo-choo went the little train, and the baby said night night."""
blocks.check:
import re
assert pattern is not None, "Write a pattern string."
exp = ["loveth", "abideth", "giveth", "taketh", "bloweth", "listeth"]
assert verbs == exp, f"Expected only the verbs {exp}. You have {verbs}. Put `(?!...)` right after `\\b`, before `[a-z]+eth\\b`."
t2 = "The fiftieth man speaketh; Macbeth's teeth."
got = re.findall(pattern, t2, flags=re.IGNORECASE)
assert "fiftieth" not in [w.lower() for w in got], "Your pattern lists the words one by one. Block the whole -ieth family with a lookahead like (?![a-z]*ieth\\b) so fiftieth, thirtieth and so on are all excluded."
blocks.solution:
import re

pattern = r"\b(?!(?:teeth|elizabeth)\b)(?![a-z]*ieth\b)[a-z]+eth\b"
verbs = re.findall(pattern, text, flags=re.IGNORECASE)

print(verbs)
hints: Two lookaheads can sit side by side after `\b`: one for the word list, one for the -ieth pattern.
`(?!(?:teeth|elizabeth)\b)` blocks those two words; `(?![a-z]*ieth\b)` blocks every ordinal.
blocks.success: Now compare this with Homework 1 Part 2: on the tagged Brown corpus, `[a-z]+eth/VBZ` gets the same verbs with no lookaheads at all. That's the "tagged vs raw" point of the whole homework.

sections.heading: From counts to rates: per 1,000 words and TTR

blocks.body: A count divided by the corpus size. **Per 1,000 words** = count / total × 1000. It's the only fair way to compare a 14k-word genre with a 182k-word one.
Number of **different** words (types) ÷ number of **words** (tokens). `len(set(words)) / len(words)`. Only compare TTRs of texts of the same size.

blocks.title: Your turn: rate and TTR
blocks.task: `words` is a list of lowercase words (no punctuation). Compute `per_1000`, how often **the** appears per 1,000 words, and `ttr`, the type-token ratio.
blocks.starter:
per_1000 = None
ttr = None

print(round(per_1000, 1), round(ttr, 3))
blocks.setup:
# A tiny Brown-style sample: a list of (word, tag) pairs, like brown.tagged_words()
tagged = [
    ("The", "AT"), ("detective", "NN"), ("walked", "VBD"), ("slowly", "RB"), ("back", "RB"),
    ("to", "IN"), ("the", "AT"), ("house", "NN"), (".", "."),
    ("He", "PPS"), ("was", "BEDZ"), ("so", "QL"), ("tired", "JJ"), ("that", "CS"), ("he", "PPS"),
    ("sat", "VBD"), ("down", "RP"), ("again", "RB"), (".", "."),
    ("So", "RB"), ("the", "AT"), ("case", "NN"), ("was", "BEDZ"), ("closed", "VBN"), (",", ","),
    ("and", "CC"), ("he", "PPS"), ("never", "RB"), ("looked", "VBD"), ("back", "RB"), (".", "."),
    ("She", "PPS"), ("left", "VBD"), ("early", "RB"), ("so", "CS"), ("she", "PPS"), ("could", "MD"),
    ("rest", "VB"), (".", "."),
]

words = [w.lower() for w, t in tagged if w.isalpha()]
blocks.check:
assert per_1000 is not None and ttr is not None, "Replace both `None`s."
n = len(words)
assert abs(per_1000 - words.count("the") / n * 1000) < 1e-6, f"'the' appears {words.count('the')} times in {n} words, so {words.count('the') / n * 1000:.1f} per 1,000. You have {per_1000}."
assert abs(ttr - len(set(words)) / n) < 1e-9, f"TTR = {len(set(words))} types / {n} tokens = {len(set(words)) / n:.3f}. You have {ttr}. Types are `len(set(words))`."
blocks.solution:
per_1000 = words.count("the") / len(words) * 1000
ttr = len(set(words)) / len(words)

print(round(per_1000, 1), round(ttr, 3))
hints: `words.count("the")` counts one word; `len(words)` is the total.
A `set` drops duplicates, so `len(set(words))` is the number of types.
blocks.success: These two numbers are columns in the Lecture 7 notebook's diversity table (TTR, per-1,000).

sections.heading: Showing results: a pandas table and a bar chart

blocks.body: pandas' table: rows and named columns. Build one from a list of dictionaries (one per row): `pd.DataFrame([{"word": "the", "count": 3}, ...])`. Print it with `df.to_string(index=False)`.

blocks.title: Your turn: a ranked table
blocks.task: Make `df`, a DataFrame with columns **word**, **count**, **per_1000** for the 5 most common words in `words`, sorted from most to least common.
blocks.starter:
import pandas as pd
from collections import Counter

rows = []
for word, count in Counter(words).most_common(5):
    pass   # add a dictionary to rows

df = None
print(df.to_string(index=False))
blocks.setup:
# A tiny Brown-style sample: a list of (word, tag) pairs, like brown.tagged_words()
tagged = [
    ("The", "AT"), ("detective", "NN"), ("walked", "VBD"), ("slowly", "RB"), ("back", "RB"),
    ("to", "IN"), ("the", "AT"), ("house", "NN"), (".", "."),
    ("He", "PPS"), ("was", "BEDZ"), ("so", "QL"), ("tired", "JJ"), ("that", "CS"), ("he", "PPS"),
    ("sat", "VBD"), ("down", "RP"), ("again", "RB"), (".", "."),
    ("So", "RB"), ("the", "AT"), ("case", "NN"), ("was", "BEDZ"), ("closed", "VBN"), (",", ","),
    ("and", "CC"), ("he", "PPS"), ("never", "RB"), ("looked", "VBD"), ("back", "RB"), (".", "."),
    ("She", "PPS"), ("left", "VBD"), ("early", "RB"), ("so", "CS"), ("she", "PPS"), ("could", "MD"),
    ("rest", "VB"), (".", "."),
]

words = [w.lower() for w, t in tagged if w.isalpha()]
blocks.check:
import pandas as pd
from collections import Counter
assert df is not None, "Make `df = pd.DataFrame(rows)`."
assert list(df.columns) == ["word", "count", "per_1000"], f"The columns should be word, count, per_1000 in that order. You have {list(df.columns)}."
top = Counter(words).most_common(5)
assert list(df["count"]) == [c for w, c in top], f"The counts should be {[c for w, c in top]}. You have {list(df['count'])}."
assert abs(df["per_1000"].iloc[0] - top[0][1] / len(words) * 1000) < 1e-6, "per_1000 should be count / len(words) * 1000."
blocks.solution:
import pandas as pd
from collections import Counter

rows = []
for word, count in Counter(words).most_common(5):
    rows.append({"word": word, "count": count, "per_1000": count / len(words) * 1000})

df = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print(df.to_string(index=False))
hints: Each row is a dictionary with the three keys: `{"word": word, "count": count, "per_1000": ...}`.
`rows.append({...})` inside the loop, then `df = pd.DataFrame(rows)` after it.
blocks.success: This is exactly how the Lecture 7 notebook's `display_top_words` builds its tables.

blocks.title: Your turn: a horizontal bar chart
blocks.task: Plot the 5 most common words as a **horizontal bar chart** (`ax.barh`), **most common at the top**, with the x-axis labeled **count**.
blocks.starter:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from collections import Counter

top = Counter(words).most_common(5)
labels = [w for w, c in top]
counts = [c for w, c in top]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3))
# bars, flip so the biggest is on top, label the x-axis

plt.show()

import _sc
a = _sc.last().axes[0]
assert a.patches, "No bars yet. Use `ax.barh(labels, counts)`."
assert len(a.patches) == 5, f"There should be 5 bars. You have {len(a.patches)}."
assert a.yaxis_inverted(), "The biggest bar is at the bottom. Flip it with `ax.invert_yaxis()`."

blocks.solution:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from collections import Counter

top = Counter(words).most_common(5)
labels = [w for w, c in top]
counts = [c for w, c in top]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3))
ax.barh(labels, counts)
ax.invert_yaxis()
ax.set_xlabel('count')

plt.show()
hints: `ax.barh(labels, counts)` draws horizontal bars.
`barh` puts the first item at the bottom; `ax.invert_yaxis()` flips it.

exercises.prompt: What is `counts.get("zebra", 0)` if "zebra" was never counted?
hints: Read each option out loud and cross off the ones that are clearly wrong.

choices.feedback: Right: the second argument is the default when the key is missing.
That's what `counts["zebra"]` would do; `.get` avoids it.
Only if you leave out the default.

exercises.title: Why does it match everything?
hints: Read each option out loud and cross off the ones that are clearly wrong.
The chapter's cards in this section have the exact fact you need.
Pick the one that matches the definition word for word.
solution: Think about where the regex is standing when it reaches `(?!eth)`.
After `[a-zA-Z]+`, it's already past the word.
exercises.why: Lookaheads guard what comes next, so put them before the part they're about.

choices.text: The lookahead checks what comes after the whole word (a space), which is never 'eth'
choices.feedback: Right: `+` eats the word first, then the lookahead looks past it.
They work; this one is just in the wrong place.
That would make it match even empty strings.

exercises.title: What does \1 match?
hints: Read each option out loud and cross off the ones that are clearly wrong.
The chapter's cards in this section have the exact fact you need.
Pick the one that matches the definition word for word.
solution: It refers back to a group.
Same text, not same kind of text.
exercises.why: Backreferences are how regex finds repetition.

choices.text: Exactly the same text group 1 matched
choices.feedback: Right: it's a copy of whatever group 1 captured.
That would be `\w+` again, which allows different words.
In a pattern, `\1` is a backreference, not a digit.
